subject: optimization step in bayesian model with Stan

messages.author: 59d88f6154d1c24c
messages.subject: optimization step in bayesian model with Stan
parts:
Hi,

I am new to Stan and I am trying to implement a model that has an optimisation step inside the likelihood. The model is like that :

likelihood= prod (w_i), where w_i = (e^lambda*(x-t))/sum((e^lambda*(x-t)) --> it is softmax function, with argument lambda*(x-t)

and we have the optimization step that lambda : sum(w_i*(x-t))=0 (which I don't know how to implement in Stan)

the prior is t ~ normal (0,1)

I tried the following, but it does not seem to converge, R:hat is too big:

emplik.model='
functions {
  real emplik_log(vector y, real t, real lambda){
    return sum(log_softmax(lambda*(y-t)));
  }
}
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  real lambda;
  real t;
}
transformed parameters {
  real empkum;
  empkum <- sum(exp(lambda*(y-t)));
}
model {
  increment_log_prob(empkum);
  t ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ emplik(t, lambda);
}
'
sample=80
prior_mean=0# prior expectation
prior_var=1
lvar=1
prior_theta=rnorm(1, mean=prior_mean, sd=sqrt(prior_var))
x=rnorm(sample, mean=prior_theta, sd=sqrt(lvar))

emplik.data<-list(N=sample, y=x) 
emplik.mcmc<-stan(model_code="emplik.model", data=emplik.data, iter=100, chains=4)
print(emplik.mcmc, param="emplik")

Thanks for information, it's still a pity, I things such optimization steps woule be well suited in C++, maybe better that what we obtain with R.

They are well suited and Stan even has pretty good optimization algorithms with automatic differentiation built in. You just can't do optimization (or quadrature or root-finding) within the transformed parameters or model block currently.

Ben

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: optimization step in bayesian model with Stan
parts:
However, if the OP is desperate enough, a fixed number of
optimization steps for eg Newton-Raphson could be implemented
explicitly in Stan. If the problem itself is known and
well-behaved, 4-8 steps could provide convergence that is
indistinguisable from an optimization routine (it would be a bit
slower because of not terminating early).

I did not do the analysis for this problem, but I guess it is
worth an experiment.

Stan can be coaxed to do a number of things that are not
explicitly available built-in. Eg currently I am using an
closed-form formula for a matrix exponential (matrix is small,
<7x7, and sparse). Suboptimal and tedious, yes, but doable.

Best,

Tamas
